text.p: Following are thumbnail sketches of the key personalities in the French parliamentary election, called for May 25 and June 1:
PRESIDENT JACQUES CHIRAC
Chirac, 64, a Gaullist, reached the goal of a 30-year career by winning the presidency over Socialist Lionel Jospin in May 1995, after two failed bids in 1981 and 1988.

His decision to call a snap election fits his image as a fighter who loves challenges. The gamble could ensure smooth sailing for the five remaining years of his seven-year term, or doom his presidency by making him a lame duck prematurely.

A graduate of the elite civil service school, Chirac entered government at 34 under his mentor, General Charles de Gaulle, making his mark as a farm minister. He became prime minister at 41 and resigned two years later in 1976.

The founder of the Gaullist Rally for the Republic (RPR) in 1976, he was elected mayor of Paris in 1977. He split the right-wing vote in his first presidential bid, helping ensure the election of the late Socialist Francois Mitterrand.
When the centre-right won 1986 parliamentary elections, he became prime minister in an unprecedented power sharing with Mitterrand who beat him to the presidency in 1988.

As president, he weathered a worldwide furore by ordering a final series of nuclear tests. Elected on promises to curb high uemployment, he soon turned around to order budget austerity to ensure France's entry into the single European currency in 1999.
He also abolished conscription, shook up the armed forces and moved France closer to the NATO alliance, while challenging U.S. dominance in European security and the Middle East.
PRIME MINISTER ALAIN JUPPE

Juppe has set records as the least popular prime minister in France's Fifth Republic after starting out with a record approval rating for a new premier when newly-elected Gaullist President Jacques Chirac appointed him in May 1995.
A brilliant mind with the image of an unfeeling technocrat, the 51-year-old Juppe is also president of the Gaullist RPR party founded by Chirac.
He incurred public anger and triggered labour unrest with an austerity drive to cut public deficits to three percent of gross domestic product to qualify for a European monetary union.

Juppe's plan to curb welfare spending and overhaul the loss-making SNCF state railway sparked a 24-day public service strike in November and December 1995. He maintained the core reforms but abandoned plans to make civil servants work longer for a full pension.

He increased the tax burden by some 120 billion francs to a record 45.7 percent of gross domestic product in his first 15 months in office, but has since begun a five-year programme of income tax cuts, abolishing dozens of special exemptions.
His privatisation efforts have had mixed success.
A highly respected foreign minister in 1993-95, Juppe joined Chirac as a speechwriter in 1976 and served as budget minister in his 1986-88 government before becoming RPR secretary-general.

His image of integrity suffered over 1995 revelations that he had obtained luxury city-owned apartments for himself and family members at below-market rents when Chirac was mayor of Paris and he was finance director.
SOCIALIST PARTY LEADER LIONEL JOSPIN
Jospin, 59, has managed to unite his fractious party behind him, but he has yet to shake off the "decent loser" tag he earned by narrowly losing the presidency to Jacques Chirac in 1995.
Silver-haired and bespectacled, he has a stilted, professorial manner. Surveys show voters perceive him as genuine and honest.

He has projected a new conbativeness ahead of the snap elections, launching a personal attack on Prime Minister Alain Juppe as "arrogant and authoritarian". Jospin has also sounded lukewarm on plans for a single European currency in an attempt to woo the Communists into an electoral pact.

The son of a schoolteacher, he had a strict Protestant upbringing and attended the elite National Administrative College (ENA) and joined the Foreign Ministry, before dropping out to become an economics lecturer.

In 1981, he succeeded Francois Mitterrand as first secretary of the Socialist party after Mitterrand was elected president. When Mitterrand was re-elected in 1988, he became education minister, serving until 1992.
Jospin led his own faction in the divided party, feuding with Laurent Fabius and Michel Rocard in a bitter 1990 congress.

After a period in the political wilderness, he was chosen by grassroots members as the Socialists' surprise presidential candidate in 1995 after European Commission president Jacques Delors decided not to stand.
He took over from Henri Emmanuelli as party leader after the election.
